# Wisdom of Solomon Chapter 6 — Disagreement Log

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Agents:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Total Disagreements:** 13

---

## Disagreement 1 — Verse 2: "proud of many nations" vs. "take pride in the numbers"

- **EMET:** "proud of many nations"
- **LOGOS:** "take pride in the numbers of your nations"
- **PNEUMA:** "pride themselves on commanding many nations"
- **Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts LOGOS — "numbers of your nations" preserves the plēthos (multitude/number) aspect; PNEUMA adds "commanding" not in the text.

---

## Disagreement 2 — Verse 3: "given to you from the Lord" vs. "given to you by the Lord"

- **EMET:** "dominion was given to you from the Lord"
- **LOGOS:** "authority was given to you by the Lord"
- **PNEUMA:** "authority you hold was given to you by the Lord"
- **Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "given to you by the Lord" — ek kyriou means "from/by the Lord"; preposition "by" is more natural in English for agency.

---

## Disagreement 3 — Verse 5: "severe judgment" vs. "strict judgment"

- **EMET:** "a severe judgment falls on those in high places"
- **LOGOS:** "strict judgment is reserved for those who stand in high places"
- **PNEUMA:** "severe judgment waits for those who occupy the high places"
- **Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "strict judgment" (LOGOS) — exetasis pikrotatē means literally "the bitterest examination"; "strict" better conveys the rigorous quality; "severe" is acceptable but less precise.

---

## Disagreement 4 — Verse 6: "tested" vs. "called to account"

- **EMET:** "mighty men will be mightily tested"
- **LOGOS:** "the mighty will be mightily called to account"
- **PNEUMA:** "the powerful will face a powerful reckoning"
- **Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "called to account" (LOGOS) — exetasthēsontai is from exetazō (to examine juridically); "tested" (EMET) is too neutral; PNEUMA's "reckoning" is strong but noun-based, losing the passive examination sense.

---

## Disagreement 5 — Verse 7: "show no partiality" vs. "not impressed by anyone's person"

- **EMET:** "will show no partiality" (ou leptourgēsei prosōpon)
- **LOGOS:** "is not impressed by anyone's person"
- **PNEUMA:** "is not swayed by anyone's status"
- **Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "is not impressed by anyone's person" — prosōpolēmpsia (face-taking/partiality) is a Jewish ethical term; LOGOS captures both the Greek term and the concept; "not swayed by status" (PNEUMA) is good but loses the "face/person" image.

---

## Disagreement 6 — Verse 10: "kept holy things in a holy way" vs. "guarded holy things in a holy manner"

- **EMET:** "have kept holy things in a holy way" (hosiōs hosia tērēsantes)
- **LOGOS:** "have guarded holy things in a holy manner"
- **PNEUMA:** "kept what is holy in a holy way"
- **Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "guarded holy things in a holy manner" — tēreō means to guard/keep/watch over; "guarded" is more active than "kept"; the wordplay hosiōs hosia (holily holy-things) should be noted.

---

## Disagreement 7 — Verse 12: "readily perceived" vs. "easily perceived"

- **EMET:** "easily perceived"
- **LOGOS:** "readily perceived"
- **PNEUMA:** "makes herself accessible"
- **Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "readily perceived" — PNEUMA's rendering shifts to Wisdom's action (she makes herself accessible) but the Greek describes the lover's perception of her; "readily" is more natural than "easily" in this register.

---

## Disagreement 8 — Verse 14: "sitting at his gates" vs. "seated at his very gate"

- **EMET:** "sitting at his gates" (pro tōn thyrōn)
- **LOGOS:** "seated at his very gate"
- **PNEUMA:** "sitting at his door"
- **Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "seated at his very gate" — the participle kathēmenē suggests settled waiting; "seated" is more dignified for Wisdom personified than "sitting"; "very gate" emphasizes proximity.

---

## Disagreement 9 — Verse 16: "graciously appears to them" vs. "meets them graciously"

- **EMET:** "she graciously appears to them on their paths"
- **LOGOS:** "she meets them graciously on their paths"
- **PNEUMA:** "she meets them, full of grace, on their way"
- **Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "she meets them graciously on their paths" — hypanta means to meet/encounter; EMET's "appears" is passive; LOGOS's "meets" preserves the active encounter; PNEUMA's "full of grace" is an expansion.

---

## Disagreement 10 — Verse 17: "most sincere desire" vs. "genuine desire"

- **EMET:** "the most sincere desire for instruction"
- **LOGOS:** "the genuine desire for instruction"
- **PNEUMA:** "a genuine desire to be taught"
- **Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "genuine desire for instruction" — gnēsia paideias epithumia; "genuine" captures gnēsia (authentic/legitimate); "most sincere" (EMET) overstates the superlative; PNEUMA's "to be taught" shifts paideia from education to a passive receiving.

---

## Disagreement 11 — Verse 18: "assurance of immortality" vs. "guarantee of imperishability"

- **EMET:** "the assurance of immortality" (athanasias)
- **LOGOS:** "the guarantee of imperishability" (aphtharsia)
- **PNEUMA:** "the guarantee of imperishability"
- **Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "guarantee of imperishability" — aphtharsia is the consistent term used in this book (cf. 2:23); EMET uses "immortality" (athanasia) which is a different word; LOGOS is textually more accurate here.

---

## Disagreement 12 — Verse 23: envy formulation

- **EMET:** "travel with sickly envy"
- **LOGOS:** "make my way with consuming envy"
- **PNEUMA:** "be twisted by envy in the telling"
- **Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "make my way with consuming envy" (LOGOS) — phthonos means wasting/consuming envy; the verb synodeuō means to travel with/accompany; LOGOS renders both elements precisely; "sickly" (EMET) and "twisted" (PNEUMA) are interpretive.

---

## Disagreement 13 — Verse 24: "salvation of the world" vs. "welfare of the world"

- **EMET:** "the salvation of the world"
- **LOGOS:** "the welfare of the world"
- **PNEUMA:** "the flourishing of the world depends on..."
- **Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "welfare of the world" — sōtēria in a political-philosophical context means safety/welfare/preservation; "salvation" carries theological connotations inappropriate here; PNEUMA's "flourishing" is excellent but too broad.
